center: On Sunday, March 9, in Manhattan, jurors convicted Oren Alexander, Tal Alexander, and Alon Alexander on all 10 counts after a five-week trial that began deliberations Thursday.

Prosecutors say the Alexander brothers carried out a sex-trafficking conspiracy from around 2008 to 2021 using luxury promises, leading to their December 2024 arrests at Brooklyn's Metropolitan Detention Center.

NEW YORK — Three brothers, including two of the nation's most successful luxury real estate brokers, were convicted of sex trafficking Monday after a five-week trial over accusations that they drugged and raped scores of women they had dazzled with their wealth and opulent lifestyle.
The verdict came after 11 women testified in Manhattan federal court they were sexually assaulted by one or more of the brothers: twins Oren and Alon Alexander, 38, and Tal Alexander, 39. All three shook their heads as the jury foreperson said "guilty" 19 straight times, a powerful reckoning that could put them behind bars for the rest of their lives.
Tal Alexander dropped his head into his crossed arms. Their stunned parents sat in the gallery behind them. Alon Alexander's wife shielded her face with her hand and appeared to fight back tears.
Judge Valerie E. Caproni set sentencing for Aug. 6. The brothers, jailed since their 2024 arrests, will appeal the verdict, their lawyers said.
"We believe in our clients' innocence and we're not going to stop fighting until we prevail, and we believe that we will one day prevail," defense lawyer Marc Agnifilo said outside the courthouse.
U.S. Attorney Jay Clayton lauded the verdict as vindication for victims of crimes that often go unreported and unpunished.
"The truth is sex trafficking and other federal sex offenses are present in many walks of life and we have not done enough to root it out," Clayton said in a statement.
The verdict represented a spectacular fall for Oren and Tal Alexander, once known as real estate's "A Team" for their high-ticket sales and celebrity clientele. After smashing sales records at industry powerhouse Douglas Elliman, the brothers started their own firm. Alon Alexander ran their family's private security company.
Victims testified that they met the brothers at nightclubs, parties and on dating apps, and were attacked after accepting their invitations to all-expense paid getaways to the Hamptons; Aspen, Colorado; and a Caribbean cruise. More than 60 women say they were raped by one or more of the brothers, according to prosecutors.
Defense lawyers suggested the accusers had faulty memories or were hoping to cash in on the brothers' fortunes. The brothers were womanizers, their lawyers conceded. But they insisted any sex was consensual.
In addition to the top charges, Alon and Tal Alexander were also convicted of sex trafficking of a minor while Alon and Oren Alexander were convicted of aggravated sexual abuse by force or intoxicant and sexual abuse of a physically incapacitated person. Oren Alexander was also convicted of sexually exploiting a minor after prosecutors showed the jury a video he recorded of himself appearing to assault a drugged 17-year-old.
Besides the criminal case, the brothers have faced about two dozen lawsuits over the last two years, including one filed last week in which a real estate reality star alleges Oren Alexander drugged and assaulted her while she was in New York City for a real estate event.
When the first of the lawsuits were filed, multiple women came forward claiming they had also been assaulted, and that the brothers' misconduct had been an open secret in the real estate world. The government took notice and opened a criminal case.
During the trial, many women who testified said they believed the brothers had spiked their drinks. Some described feeling like they'd lost control of their bodies.
One woman testified that she met the brothers in 2012 at a party at actor Zac Efron's Manhattan apartment. She said she had almost no interaction with the actor, who was not accused of any misdeeds, and went to a nightclub later in the night before waking up naked with a nude Alon Alexander standing over her.
"I don't want to have sex with you," she testified telling him. "Haha, you already did," she recalled him snapping back as he "laughed in my face."
Prosecutors pushed back against the idea that the accusers were hoping to cash in on lawsuits. Only two have lawsuits pending, prosecutor Elizabeth Espinosa told jurors, and both are wealthy.
One woman who testified said she was raped by Alon Alexander in Aspen, Colorado, in 2017, when she was 17. She said she was the daughter of a billionaire.
"I don't want their money. I just don't want them to have it," she told jurors.
An artist and gallery owner testified she was raped by Tal Alexander and another man at a home in the Hamptons in 2011 after taking a drink that left her feeling paralyzed.
The woman said she sued last year even though she will "never need their money" because the Alexanders "kept calling us gold diggers, shake down artists, con artists."
"If there's a kid with a stick who keeps hitting people, you take their stick away," she told the jury. "Money is their stick, so you take it away so they can't hurt people anymore."

Alexander brothers found guilty of all counts in sex trafficking trial
sources.text:
Alexander brothers found guilty of all counts in sex trafficking trial
NEW YORK — Three brothers, including two who were among the country’s most prominent real estate brokers, were convicted in New York on Monday of engaging in a yearslong conspiracy to traffic women and girls for sex.
The brothers — Tal and Oren Alexander, who regularly closed multimillion-dollar real estate deals in New York and elsewhere, and Alon Alexander, a security executive — were found guilty on every count they each faced, and could now all face life in prison when they are sentenced on Aug. 6.
ADVERTISING
The verdict comes more than a month after the trial began in U.S. District Court in Manhattan where the six-woman, six-man jury heard weeks of emotional and often graphic testimony from 11 women who accused the Alexander brothers of rape or sexual assault. Jurors deliberated for 21 hours.
In some cases, the brothers — Tal, 39, and Oren and Alon, twins who are 38 — used drugs to incapacitate their victims before raping them.
In one case, prosecutors showed the jury a video of Oren Alexander raping an incapacitated 17-year-old girl in 2009 in a Manhattan apartment he shared with his brothers. Although courtroom spectators were not able to see the video, Andrews Jones, one of the prosecutors, described it in his summation — how Oren Alexander set up the front-facing camera on his laptop, adjusted its angle and then got into bed with the drugged girl.
“When you saw him pick up her limp legs and climb on top of her lifeless body, you knew what you were seeing,” Jones said.
The victim, who testified under a pseudonym, said she had no memory of the events shown in the video or of ever meeting Oren Alexander.
In court, none of the three brothers testified at the trial.
Their lawyers, summing up their cases to the jury, argued that the brothers were “playboys” and “womanizers” but not criminals. They cast the dozens of accusers as a bloc of scorned women, all motivated by shame, regret and greed. Their incomplete recollections, the lawyers said, were due not to drugs slipped to them by the brothers, but their own voluntary consumption of alcohol and narcotics. Their accounts of being assaulted, the lawyers argued, were influenced by media reports and cash-hungry civil lawyers, who had whipped up a conspiracy.
They were not successful in persuading the jury.
The verdict seals a spectacular fall from grace for the Alexander brothers, one that has been breathlessly chronicled by tabloids and real estate publications since allegations first surfaced against them nearly two years ago.
When the trial opened in January, the brothers were together facing 12 charges. But late in the trial, prosecutors dropped two counts, telling the judge they had been forced to do so after one accuser became so frightened by the defense team’s tactics that she refused to testify. Prosecutors said in a memo to the judge that a private investigator hired by the defense had pretended to be an insurance agent, visited the woman’s neighborhood and asked questions about her children.
The conduct “crossed ethical lines,” prosecutors said. It also followed a pattern of shame and intimidation tactics employed by the brothers since the first accusations against them were made public in the summer of 2024.
In the end, they faced 10 counts, and were found guilty on every one of them.
Those accusations — two civil lawsuits first reported on by The Real Deal, a real estate trade publication — prompted an avalanche of litigation against the brothers. By the time federal charges were filed in December 2024, with all three men arrested in predawn raids in Miami, prosecutors would say they had interviewed 60 women while preparing their case.

The building at 281 Park Avenue South, with its granite base and mansard roof, reeked of old money. Turreted corners. Arched windows. Limestone that looked as if it had just surfaced from the bottom of the ocean.
If you were launching a new firm and wanted to convey permanence, stability, and the sort of institutional gravitas that spans centuries, not a couple of months, the building would do a lot of the heavy lifting. Which is why it made perfect sense for the founders of Official to hold their first event there, in October 2022.
Official was not like other real estate brokerages of the era, defined by reality TV stars who might jump in a swimming pool to celebrate a closing. They were discreet. Exclusive. They liked to say that they built a moat around the firm. Only agents who had done $1 billion in sales could apply to work there.
The firm would operate like a private office—part agent, part portfolio manager, part lifestyle concierge—serving the top fraction of the top one percent, people whose wealth was so vast they were constantly involved in real estate transactions. This was meant to be a business built to last, one that transcended the typical churn of the brokerage world.
The firm had five founders, all heavyweights in ultra-luxury real estate, but the rainmakers, and the de facto faces of the brand, were the Alexander brothers: Tal and Oren, just 11 months apart in age. The brothers looked the part—Tom Ford, Armani, bodies honed by yoga and personal trainers—but their meteoric rise had not been built on discretion. Quite the opposite. They had aggressively courted the press to build their brand and used Instagram to show that they were more than what Oren dismissively referred to as “real estate peddlers.”
Instead, they lived the lives of their clients. Formula 1 races in Monaco. The opening ceremonies of the World Cup in Doha. Parties in Ibiza. They were selling to their friends. Now, in their mid-thirties, having set records for residential real estate closings in New York and London and Miami, they had entered what their peers at Official saw as a more mature phase. They didn’t need the press. In fact, Oren said he tried to avoid it. His clients preferred it that way.
If Official were to fulfill its promise, it would have to function like a white shoe law firm, not a cutthroat real estate brokerage that operated like an old boys’ club or, worse, a frat—meaning the Alexanders would have to clean up their act. The other founders didn’t want the brothers to lose their edge, but they would have to become more collaborative. “They had a reputation for being assholes,” a former colleague said.
They also had a reputation for womanizing that had long followed Tal and Oren, as well as Oren’s twin, Alon, who ran the New York branch of the family security firm. “It was like the worst-kept awful secret that those brothers together… Like, you do not let female agents, female clients, your mom, sister, or daughter anywhere near them,” said a rival agent. “You just keep your eyes on your own problems, your own work, and you just move forward. And you hope you never have to interact with them.”
But no one foresaw what came next. In March 2024 two women separately sued Oren and Alon for sexual assault, setting off a deluge of accusations that was followed by an FBI investigation, which culminated in the arrest of all three brothers on December 11, 2024.
This January in Manhattan the Alexanders went on trial for 12 felony counts related to federal sex trafficking. The government later dropped two of the charges after those victims went quiet due to what prosecutors characterize as witness intimidation. The defense attorneys say the alleged intimidation came from private investigators who have been fired by the defense team and was not sanctioned. The brothers pleaded not guilty, but in March they were convicted of all 10 counts.
“They have never sex-trafficked anyone, never drugged anyone, and never engaged in nonconsensual sexual conduct,” said Juda Engelmayer, a public relations strategist (known for representing Harvey Weinstein) who has been hired by the Alexanders and spoke to T&C just before the verdict came down. “They are innocent.”
Now that the federal trial is over, Alon and Oren still face state sexual battery charges in Miami, including one charge that stems from an alleged incident at Alon’s Miami Beach condo on New Year’s Eve 2016. They have pleaded not guilty to these, too. It may take years for all the cases to be resolved, but already the scandal has prompted a quiet reckoning within the world of luxury real estate.
How the Alexander brothers reached the uppermost tier of their industry, bringing in billions of dollars in revenue, is a story of ambition, hard work, and a knack for being in the right room at the right time. But if the allegations in these civil and criminal cases against them are true—something the brothers vigorously dispute—their rise was shadowed by a darkness that remained hidden not in spite of their success but perhaps because of it.
The origin story of the Alexanders, the one they liked to tell, was about hustle. It elided their privileged upbringing in Miami and the fact that their father helped make some of their biggest deals, but it did have the benefit of being true. “We were never given anything,” Oren said in a 2022 episode of the YouTube series From the Founder. Their father, an Israeli immigrant, gave them a taste of the good life but taught them they’d have to earn it for themselves. He ran a security firm that provided guards for gated communities and parties at the Versace mansion. By the time the boys were teenagers, it was one of the largest security contractors in South Florida. Shabbat dinner, Oren said, was more like a board meeting. “We talked business all the time,” he said.
They grew up in Bal Harbour, a ritzy village at the north end of Miami Beach, in a Mediterranean-style mansion that sits on the water. They had a pool in the back yard and were part of a clique of rich, popular boys who went to Michael M. Krop, a large public high school. They often hung out with the kids from the local private schools—Miami Country Day, Ransom Everglades—and held rowdy parties at their 6,000-square-foot home while their parents slept at the other end of the house.
After high school Tal went to Hofstra University to play tennis. A year later, in 2005, Oren left for the University of Colorado and Alon the University of Maryland. By 2008 they were all in New York. Alon, after graduating from the NYU School of Law, would eventually go into the family security business. Tal and Oren gravitated toward real estate.
At 21, Oren caught his first big break, when he sold an $8.2 million penthouse at the Park Imperial to an attorney he had met skiing in Aspen. It became a sort of model for the brothers to follow: Figure out where the money is. Get an invite, get a table, get on the same ski lift, and, whenever necessary, get on a plane. “It wasn’t just going to the event,” Oren would later recall on From the Founder. “It was, ‘What do these people look like? Where are they in the room?’…It was like Wedding Crashers: ‘Tal, that developer by the bar? Go!’”
By 2015 Oren and Tal were rooming together in a 4,200-square-foot condo in the New Museum building (Jon Bon Jovi had sold his penthouse atop the building for $37.5 million the year before). “It shows that we live like our clients, which is very important to our business,” Oren told Business Insider in 2015. “They trust us because we not only do it for work, we also engage in it in our lifestyle, and that’s always been our competitive advantage.” They boned up on fine art and went to Art Basel in Switzerland, the Biennale in Venice, and Frieze in London. They took clients to lunch at Sadelle’s, Lure Fishbar, and Harry Cipriani, where Oren bragged he could “get the number one table anytime I want.”
“You can see everyone who walks in and walks out,” Tal told Business Insider. “I can’t even tell you how much wealth was there last Friday,” Oren added. They aggressively befriended brokers of yachts and private jets, architects, designers, wealth managers—anyone who could refer them business. They were rapidly becoming two of the biggest stars at Douglas Elliman, one of the largest luxury real estate firms in the U.S.
A colleague at the time said Oren had a “vapid nature to him,” and that both brothers came across as not that bright. But it didn’t matter. When it came to selling real estate, they were machines. “I’ve worked with hundreds, maybe thousands of agents. I’ve never seen anybody operate like that,” says a former colleague. “It was all business, all the time, 24 hours a day. You could call Oren at two o’clock in the morning, four o’clock in the morning, the phone’s right next to him. I saw that shit with my own eyes. They were successful because they worked harder than everybody else.”
Inspired by The Wolf of Wall Street and the idea of chop shops and dialing for dollars, in 2019 they paid someone who promised he could get them the phone number of anyone in Manhattan. The brothers had realized there was a correlation between art collectors and the clientele they coveted. Oren came across an article in Forbes listing the top art collectors in the finance industry. “I said, ‘Perfect, I’ll take that list and give it to him,’” Oren said on From the Founder.
Using the list, Tal cold-called the hedge fund titan Ken Griffin, and a few months later the brothers had helped close the most expensive piece of residential real estate in U.S. history: a 24,000-square-foot penthouse that spanned floors 50 through 53 at 220 Central Park South. It sold for $238 million. Now certified rock stars in the industry, Oren turned his focus to Miami, while Tal stayed in New York. They called themselves the A-Team.
It was an era, fueled in part by reality TV, when real estate agents, who had long operated behind the scenes, began to see themselves as quasi-celebrities, says Rob Giem, a broker based in Southern California who Tal would later try to recruit to Official. The brothers had themselves been approached to star in a reality TV show, Tal said, but they turned it down. (Oren separately auditioned for Million Dollar Listing but didn’t make the cut.) Instead they cultivated their image as concierges to the gilded life on social media, filling their feeds with private jets, helicopter commutes, Wimbledon, and camel rides in Qatar. For Tal’s 30th birthday, the brothers hired a production company to film them partying in the Hamptons on a speedboat in white suits. They set the footage to Travis Scott’s hit “A-Team.”
“Their clients were rough, and they were rough,” says a rival New York agent. “They had a clientele that was young, wealthy assholes, and they were young and wealthy assholes. It just kind of fit that vibe. And one of the things they did was surround themselves with what their clientele liked, which was young, hot women.”
In 2021 Tal and Oren announced that they had closed more than $1.8 billion in sales that year, accounting for nearly 4 percent of Douglas Elliman’s business. Since they started the Alexander Team in 2012, they had done more than $7 billion in sales. While they had always been close to Douglas Elliman’s longtime CEO, Howard Lorber, who treated them like favored sons, the brothers began to wonder if they had outgrown the firm.
“We felt that the brand just wasn’t there with us,” Oren said in a 2022 interview with the Real Deal, an industry trade publication. “We were going to these events, and the people we were meeting, we were never proud to tell them we’re at Douglas Elliman. We were the Alexander Team, that was our brand, and that’s what differentiated us from the other 6,500 agents [at Douglas Elliman].”
What if they built a small, boutique firm focused exclusively on the top end of the market: homes $10 million and up? In the summer of 2022 the Alexanders launched Official with three other Douglas Elliman vets: Nicole Oge, who had led marketing at Elliman before leaving for WeWork; Richard Jordan, head of global markets at Elliman; and Andrew Wachtfogel, who led Elliman’s research team. They also poached some of the firm’s best agents in Miami, Manhattan, and the Hamptons.
The brothers took a call in St.-Tropez from a Bloomberg reporter to announce the launch of the firm. They were in the South of France, Tal told the reporter, on yachts and attending parties, drumming up more business for Official.
The first two lawsuits against Alon and Oren were filed in New York on March 8, 2024, by Rebecca Mandel and Kate Whiteman. Mandel alleged that she met the twins in 2009 at SL, a since-shuttered nightclub in the Meatpacking District. She was 18 at the time. According to the complaint, she continued to run into Oren and Alon at nightclubs around Manhattan until one night at SL around September 2010, when, she claimed, Alon spiked her drink, “resulting in significant impairment to her physical well-being.” Mandel alleged that the brothers convinced her to leave the club and go to their apartment, where they were throwing a party, but when she got there no one else was there, and there was no party. The brothers allegedly took turns raping her.
The second lawsuit alleged that Whiteman, an Australian, had met the twins at a Manhattan nightclub in 2008 and would frequently “see them out and about.” Oren pursued her for years, but she always declined meeting up, according to the complaint. Then, in May 2012, Oren asked her if she was planning to go to the Hamptons for Memorial Day weekend. The building where Official held its launch party in the fall of 2022, 281 Park Avenue South, is back on the market. The brothers, who faced trial for five weeks, were not all charged in every count — but each still faces up to life in prison on the conviction for the sex-trafficking conspiracy alone.
And now that their federal trial is over, Alon and Oren will also have to face three state rape charges in Miami, including one that stems from an alleged assault at Alon’s Miami Beach condo on New Year’s Eve in 2016.
Attorney Lilian Timmermann, who represents Lindsey Acree, one of the victims in the federal criminal case, called the verdict “an enormous victory” for the victims and a “measure of long-awaited justice.”
“It must also mark the start of a reckoning for rich, powerful men in America who thought their money and power had shielded them from consequences,” Timmermann, who also is representing Acree in her civil case against Oren and Tal Alexander, told the Miami Herald. “Today they know their victims won’t be silenced anymore.”
Arrested in Miami Beach
Since their arrests by the FBI on federal sex-trafficking charges in December 2024 in Miami Beach, twins Alon and Oren Alexander and Tal have been held at a criminal detention center in Brooklyn, the same lockup where music mogul Sean “Diddy” Combs was held during his sex-trafficking trial last year.
Alon had worked in the family’s security business in the Miami area, while Oren and Tal attained fame and fortune as luxury real estate brokers in New York City and Miami.
In a closing argument last week, Assistant U.S. Attorney Andrew Jones methodically revisited the testimony of 11 women who told jurors they were sexually assaulted by at least one of the brothers. Jones argued that the accounts, though delivered by women who “never have met each other and live different lives,” shared what he called “one horrific thing in common: they were raped by these men.”
Yachts, mansions, luxury trips
Jones outlined what the government characterized as an extensive pattern of sex-trafficking, from 2009 to 2021. Prosecutors allege the brothers used their wealth, social status and access to exclusive events to entice young women to private homes, yachts, mansions and luxury trips — sometimes paying for flights and high-end accommodations — before drugging and assaulting them.
“The defendants had a playbook,” Jones said, describing the use of “parties, boats, mansions, travel and accommodations” to lure women into isolated settings.
The government claims the brothers used force and drugs to incapacitate the women. Several women testified they believed their drinks had been spiked. Jurors were shown videos and text messages that prosecutors say corroborate the allegations. One video included a statement attributed to Oren Alexander: “I’m serious. I drug bitches.”
Grew up in Miami area
The brothers, whose parents own a waterfront home in Bal Harbour and other assets worth tens of millions of dollars, attended Dr. Michael M. Krop Senior High School near Aventura in the early 2000s.
They were seemingly on top of the world until 2024, when the first of more than two dozen lawsuits were filed by women alleging they sexually assaulted them. Those suits not only dredged up dark secrets dating back years but also laid the foundation for their federal criminal case.
Acree, who testified during the trial that she believed she was drugged and assaulted in the Hamptons by Tal Alexander and a friend of his, said she had mixed feelings about the verdict.
“I’m not happy because, you know, this shouldn’t ever happen in the world that we live in, but I’m feeling very patriotic right now in a time that I certainly haven’t for a while,” she said in an interview with the Herald. Acree is a Brooklyn gallery owner and artist.
Acree also said the parents of the Alexander brothers, Shlomi and Orly Alexander, walked into the Four Seasons hotel in Manhattan as she was meeting with Timmermann in the lobby after the verdict was read. She said they looked stone cold and serious.
In major U.S. cities, federal sex-trafficking investigations have become more commonplace in the era of Jeffrey Epstein and Diddy amid the #MeToo movement. But to make such cases, authorities have to show that a trafficker either physically threatened or forced women to engage in sexual activity with them or others for money to fulfill the legal definition of a commercial sex act.
In cases involving adults, prosecutors have to show that a trafficker used “force, fraud, or coercion to subject victims to engage in commercial sex” under federal law. In cases involving minors, the barriers to prosecution are not as high because the victims are under 18.
Last year, Diddy was acquitted of sex trafficking and racketeering charges in Manhattan federal court but found guilty of two counts of transportation to engage in prostitution — a mixed result for federal prosecutors in the Southern District of New York. He was sentenced to four years and two months in prison.
Before closing arguments in the Alexanders’ trial last week, federal prosecutors told judge Valerie E. Caproni that the government planned to drop two sex-trafficking charges against the brothers tied to events in the Hamptons in 2009, which left them facing 10 charges.
The defense attorneys representing Alon Alexander were Howard Srebnick, Jackie Perczek and Jason Goldman; lawyers defending Oren Alexander were Marc Agnifilo, Teny Geragos and Zach Intrater, along with Jenny Wilson; and lawyers representing Tal Alexander were Deanna Paul, Milton Williams and Alexander Kahn.
Srebnick and Perczek, former partners of the late Roy Black, as well as Wilson are the only attorneys from Miami.
Acree, Victim #1 in court records, acknowledged Kate Whiteman, the first woman who sued the brothers and was found dead last year in her native Australia. Her death was deemed “non-suspicious’’ by Australian authorities. She was 45. Whiteman was featured in the Real Deal, which first reported about the Alexander brothers.
“I just wish that she was here so she could see what a huge difference she made in so many women’s lives,” Acree said.
(Miami Herald staff writer Ana Claudia Chacin contributed to this report.)

sources.news_title: Luxury Real Estate Brokers And Their Brother Convicted In Federal Sex-trafficking Trial
sources.text:
Two high-profile luxury real estate brokers and their other brother were convicted Monday in a sex trafficking trial in which they were accused of using drugs and their influence to sexually abuse women.
Federal prosecutors said brothers Oren, Tal and Alon Alexander conspired for more than a decade to drug, sexually assault and rape women. The men were charged by federal prosecutors in Manhattan in December 2024.
A jury of six men and six women delivered the verdict Monday after a monthlong trial that featured testimony from more than 30 witnesses. They began deliberating Thursday.
Prosecutor Madison Smyser alleged in her opening statement that the three brothers worked together for years “raping women and girls … with promises of parties and trips, and when they got there the defendants raped them.”
The brothers have denied the allegations.
Eleven accusers testified. Six of them are part of the indictment against the brothers.
One victim, who testified under the pseudonym Katie Moore, said she was drugged and raped by Alon Alexander after a night out at a New York City club. Moore told the court that after she was handed a drink, her “body started to sway.”
“In that moment, it felt sudden. I know I wasn’t drunk or losing control; there was no gradual fade-out. I had never experienced that sort of loss of control of my body before,” she said.
Moore said Alon and Tal Alexander made her and her friend leave the club, and she vaguely remembered getting into a cab. She testified that the thing she remembered was “coming to” and being naked on a bed with Alon Alexander, who did not have any clothes on, standing over her.
“I tried to get out of the bed a few times, but Alon kept pushing me back down,” she said. “Finally, he sat down on the bed, and I was able to get up, and I said, ‘I don’t want to have sex with you,’ and he said, ‘You already did.’”
One of the charges against Oren Alexander is in connection with the alleged sexual exploitation of a minor. Prosecutors accused him of filming and sharing a video of an incapacitated 17-year-old girl in April 2009.
The woman, now 34, testified she had no memory of meeting Oren Alexander.
Two women testified that they felt paralyzed before they were assaulted by Oren and Alon Alexander.
The defense attempted to undermine some of the accusers’ accounts, saying the sex was consensual and suggesting that the women were motivated by disappointment and were in it for financial gain.
“Financial interest is one of the most powerful motivators. All the stories were rehearsed,” Tal Alexander’s attorney, Deanna Paul, said in her closing argument. “They’re looking for money.”
She said the women met up with the brothers “willingly” and “were free to come and go.”
“The government has not proved it was a commercial sex act because there wasn’t one, and they have failed to meet their burden,” she said.
In closing, Marc Agnifilo, Oren Alexander’s attorney, acknowledged that his client “built a lifestyle around pursuing women.”
“They hurt a lot of people’s feelings while they were ascending professionally,” he said. “They said some things that were offensive and hurtful, and we got here because of that stuff, not because they are rapists or drugged women.”
Assistant U.S. Attorney Elizabeth Espinosa said the defense was trying to confuse the jury.
“There is no good reason why all these women would commit perjury and drag their friends and family into this. Why on earth would they be here a decade later talking about their sex lives. They sat here in front of a group of strangers and detailed these horrific crimes,” she said.
The brothers had been charged in a 12-count superseding indictment. But prosecutors said one witness was intimidated and didn’t show up, so two counts were dropped, leaving 10.
The men face dozens of civil lawsuits. They have denied all allegations of misconduct. Oren and Alon Alexander are also facing criminal charges in Florida. On Thursday, a Beverly Hills real estate broker filed a civil lawsuit against Oren Alexander, alleging that he drugged and sexually assaulted her in 2014 at a dinner.
His civil attorney, Jason Goldman, said in a statement Thursday that the lawsuit was “salacious and demonstrably false” and was filed on the eve of jury deliberations as an “attempt to create headlines and taint the proceedings at a critical moment.”

sources.news_title: Alexander brothers found guilty on all counts in federal sex trafficking trial
sources.text:
The Alexander brothers were found guilty on all 10 counts in their federal sex trafficking trial.
The jury delivered its verdict on Monday, marking the end of a five-week trial where jurors heard testimony from 11 women who say they were attacked by one or more of the brothers and saw evidence, including scores of texts, emails, photos and other documents, presented by prosecutors. The jury was comprised of six men and six women and delivered the verdict after just more than two days of deliberation, which began Thursday afternoon.
Oren, Alon and Tal face a minimum sentence of 15 years and the possibility of life in prison. Judge Valerie Caproni will conduct a sentencing hearing on Aug. 6.
The brothers were convicted on 10 total counts related to sex trafficking, including conspiracy to commit sex trafficking. Prosecutors alleged that between 2008 and 2021, the Alexanders orchestrated a scheme to lure women to luxury destinations such as the Hamptons, the Bahamas and Aspen, where they and other men allegedly drugged and raped them.
Attorneys for the Alexanders said they plan to appeal, building on the objections they raised to highlight appellate issues during the trial.
The brothers’ parents called the verdict “deeply disappointing” in a statement included in the “Friends of the Alexanders” email newsletter.
“We believe there are substantial problems with the evidence and the way this case was presented. The legal process does not end here,” said the family. “We will continue fighting every day until justice is done and the three brothers regain their freedom.”
All three Alexanders were also found guilty of sex trafficking by force, fraud or coercion and inducement to travel to engage in unlawful sexual activity related to Oren’s alleged rape of Bela Koval in the Hamptons in 2016.
Tal was found guilty on one count of sex trafficking tied to the alleged rape of Lindsey Acree in the Hamptons in 2011. The jury found him guilty of sex trafficking Maya Miller in 2014 and guilty on charges that he induced Miller to travel to the Hamptons to engage in unlawful sexual activity.
Tal and Alon were found guilty of sex trafficking Isa Brooks, who was 16 years old at the time of her alleged attack in the Hamptons in 2009.
Oren and Alon were found guilty of aggravated sexual abuse and sexual abuse related to Rhonda Stone, who testified that she was drugged and raped by the twins on a 2012 cruise from Miami to the Bahamas.
Oren was found guilty of sexual exploitation of a minor. Amelia Rosen testified she was 17 years old when Oren allegedly drugged and raped her and filmed the attack.
The Alexander brothers pleaded not guilty to the charges and have denied the allegations. During their trial, attorneys for the Alexanders argued that the alleged victims who testified at trial were motivated by civil lawsuits, as well as shame and regret surrounding what they characterized as consensual sexual encounters. Only two of the women who testified — Acree and Maylen Gehret — filed lawsuits against one or more of the brothers. The other alleged victims testified under pseudonyms.
The defense attorneys pointed to inconsistencies in the women’s testimony and what they told federal investigators and their friends and family before addressing the jury. They also argued prosecutors had little evidence that the brothers surreptitiously drugged women, pointing to a lack of toxicology, medical or police reports from the time of the attacks.
The Alexanders’ attorneys put on a short case, which included testimony from a Douglas Elliman real estate agent in the Hamptons, two private chefs the brothers hired for their summer rentals in the Hamptons, and one of Alon’s ex-girlfriends.
The Alexanders have been in custody since their December 2024 arrests. They were transported to New York the following month and have since been held at the Metropolitan Detention Center in Brooklyn.
In December 2024, Oren and Alon were also charged with sexual battery in Miami-Dade County. A family friend, Ohad Fisherman, was charged in connection with one of the alleged attacks in Miami, though prosecutors dropped the charges against him in July after his trial began. Fisherman worked with Oren as a real estate agent in Miami and held his license with Official, the Side-backed brokerage firm that Oren and Tal co-founded and led until 2024.

Los abogados defensores insinuaron que las acusadoras tenían recuerdos poco fiables o que esperaban beneficiarse de la fortuna de los hermanos, de quienes sus abogados admitieron que eran mujeriegos. Pero insistieron en que cualquier relación sexual fue consensuada.
El jurado comenzó a deliberar el jueves.

Además del caso penal, el trío de hermanos enfrentaba alrededor de dos docenas de demandas, incluida una presentada el jueves por Tracy Tutor, estrella de “Million Dollar Listing Los Angeles” de Bravo. Ella alega que Oren Alexander la drogó y la agredió en el baño de un restaurante mientras ella estaba en la ciudad de Nueva York para un evento inmobiliario.
Local
Cuando comenzaron a presentarse esas demandas, varias mujeres se acercaron para afirmar que también habían sido acosadas o agredidas sexualmente, y que la mala conducta de los hermanos con las mujeres había sido un secreto a voces en el mundo inmobiliario durante años.
Durante el juicio, muchas de las mujeres que testificaron dijeron que creían haber sido drogadas después de que uno de los hermanos les ofreciera alcohol. Algunas describieron sentirse como si hubieran perdido el control de su cuerpo tras menos de una bebida.
Los hermanos conocían a las mujeres en clubes nocturnos, fiestas y aplicaciones de citas; a algunas las llevaban de viaje a destinos exclusivos y pagaban vuelos y alojamiento de lujo. Una mujer testificó que conoció a los hermanos en 2012 en una fiesta en el apartamento del actor Zac Efron en Manhattan. Dijo que casi no interactuó con el actor, a quien no se acusó de ninguna conducta indebida, y que más tarde esa noche fue a un club nocturno antes de despertarse desnuda, con Alon Alexander, también desnudo, de pie sobre ella.
Los fiscales rechazaron la idea de que las acusadoras esperaran lucrar con las demandas. Solo dos tienen demandas pendientes, dijo la fiscal Elizabeth Espinosa a los miembros del jurado, y ambas son ricas por sí mismas.
Una mujer que testificó dijo que fue violada por Alon Alexander en Aspen, Colorado, en 2017, cuando tenía 17 años. Señaló que era hija de un multimillonario. “No quiero su dinero. Lo que quiero es que no lo tengan”, dijo al jurado.
Lindsey Acree, artista y dueña de una galería en Brooklyn, testificó que fue violada por Tal Alexander y un segundo hombre en una casa en los Hamptons en el verano de 2011, después de quedar tan desorientada por beber menos de medio vaso de vino que se sintió paralizada.
La mujer, ahora de 40 años, dijo que demandó a Tal Alexander el año pasado aunque “nunca necesitará su dinero”, porque se molestó al escuchar que los Alexander “seguían llamándonos cazafortunas, extorsionadoras, estafadoras”.
“Si hay un niño con un palo que no deja de golpear a la gente, le quitas el palo”, dijo al jurado. “El dinero es su palo, así que se lo quitas para que no puedan volver a hacer daño”.
Además de los testimonios, los fiscales intentaron sustentar su caso con mensajes de texto y correos electrónicos en los que los hermanos parecían jactarse de sus hazañas sexuales y de su conocimiento sobre los efectos que diversas drogas pueden tener en las inhibiciones de una mujer, además de un blog que incluía una entrada titulada: “No es violación si ...”.
Los fiscales afirmaron que los hermanos intercambiaron correos sobre cómo introducir drogas —o “party favors”— a escondidas en un crucero, que grabaron al menos una agresión en video y que compartieron fotos de víctimas.
The Associated Press no suele identificar a personas que dicen ser víctimas de agresión sexual, a menos que decidan hacerlo públicamente, como lo han hecho Acree y Tutor.

sources.news_title: Alexander Brothers Convicted in New York Sex Trafficking Trial
sources.text:
Three prominent New York real estate figures once known for brokering multimillion-dollar luxury deals have been convicted in a federal sex trafficking case that has drawn national attention. A Manhattan federal jury found brothers Tal Alexander, Oren Alexander, and Alon Alexander guilty after hearing weeks of testimony from women who accused the men of sexual assault, coercion, and exploitation spanning several years.
The verdict marks a dramatic downfall for the Alexander brothers, who had built reputations as successful brokers in the elite New York real estate market. Prosecutors argued that the brothers abused their wealth, influence, and access to luxury social circles to lure women into situations where they were drugged, manipulated, and sexually assaulted.
High-Profile Trial in Federal Court
The case was tried in U.S. District Court in Manhattan, where federal prosecutors presented testimony from multiple women who described similar patterns of alleged abuse. According to prosecutors, the brothers targeted victims through social events, parties, and luxury trips that appeared glamorous but were allegedly used to isolate and exploit women.
Authorities said the crimes occurred in several locations including New York City, the Hamptons, Miami, and Aspen, areas frequently associated with wealthy social scenes and luxury real estate clients.
During the trial, numerous accusers took the stand and described encounters with the brothers that they said quickly turned into traumatic experiences. Some women testified that they believed they had been drugged after consuming drinks provided by one of the defendants. Others described situations in which they said they were pressured or coerced into sexual acts.
Prosecutors argued that the Alexander brothers followed a consistent pattern in which they used their status as successful real estate brokers to build trust before committing assaults.
Prosecutors Describe a Long-Running Scheme
Federal prosecutors told jurors that the defendants operated with a calculated strategy that spanned more than a decade. According to the government, the brothers invited women to exclusive gatherings and private parties, often portraying the events as elite social opportunities connected to their luxury real estate network.
Once the women were isolated, prosecutors alleged that alcohol or drugs were used to impair them, making them vulnerable to sexual assault. Prosecutors characterized the conduct as part of a broader sex trafficking operation involving manipulation, intimidation, and abuse of power.
The prosecution argued that the defendants’ wealth and professional success allowed them to avoid accountability for years while continuing to engage in predatory behavior.
Evidence presented in court included testimony from alleged victims, text messages, and other communications that prosecutors said supported the government’s claims about the brothers’ actions.
Defense Claims Encounters Were Consensual
Defense attorneys strongly disputed the allegations throughout the trial. Lawyers for the Alexander brothers argued that the encounters described by the accusers were consensual and that prosecutors had misinterpreted social interactions and relationships.
The defense also suggested that some accusations were motivated by financial incentives or civil litigation claims. Attorneys emphasized that the defendants were active in nightlife and social scenes but maintained that no criminal conduct occurred.
Despite these arguments, jurors ultimately sided with prosecutors after reviewing the evidence and testimony presented during the proceedings.
Fall From the Top of the Luxury Real Estate Market
Before their arrest, Tal and Oren Alexander were widely known in the luxury real estate industry. The brothers gained recognition for representing high-end properties and working with wealthy clients in New York and South Florida.
They had previously worked at Douglas Elliman, one of the largest residential real estate brokerage firms in the United States. The Alexanders were known for selling luxury condominiums, waterfront estates, and multimillion-dollar properties.
Their professional success helped them cultivate connections with celebrities, investors, and affluent buyers in major real estate markets. The brothers were frequently seen at exclusive social events and were considered rising stars in the competitive world of luxury real estate.
Alon Alexander, the third brother convicted in the case, was associated with the family’s private security business and also participated in the social circle described by prosecutors.
The criminal case has significantly damaged the brothers’ reputations and sent shockwaves through parts of the real estate community that once celebrated their success.
Broader Impact of the Case
The Alexander brothers’ conviction highlights growing scrutiny around allegations of sexual misconduct among high-profile professionals. Federal prosecutors have increasingly pursued cases involving abuse of power, particularly when wealth or influence may have played a role in enabling criminal behavior.
Legal analysts say the case demonstrates how prosecutors can use federal sex trafficking laws to pursue allegations involving coercion, manipulation, and exploitation rather than traditional trafficking scenarios alone.
The case also reflects a broader trend of victims coming forward years after alleged incidents occurred, often leading to both criminal investigations and civil lawsuits.
Sentencing and Next Steps
Following the guilty verdict, the Alexander brothers now face the possibility of significant prison sentences under federal law. Sex trafficking convictions can carry severe penalties, including decades behind bars depending on the charges and circumstances involved.
Sentencing will take place at a later hearing in federal court. Defense attorneys are expected to challenge the verdict and may pursue appeals as the case moves forward.
For many observers, the trial represents one of the most prominent criminal cases involving figures from the luxury real estate industry. The outcome underscores the legal consequences that can arise when prosecutors present evidence of systematic abuse and exploitation.
As the case proceeds to sentencing, it will likely continue to attract attention from both the legal community and the broader public, serving as a stark reminder that even high-profile professionals can face serious criminal accountability under federal law.
